The Election of 1932. Franklin D. Roosevelt's overwhelming victory over incumbent Herbert Hoover marked a decisive repudiation of Republican laissez-faire ideology in the depths of the Great Depression. Roosevelt won fifty-seven percent of the popular vote and four hundred seventy-two electoral votes, the largest mandate since nineteen twenty. He ran on a vague but powerful promise of a New Deal for the American people.

Herbert Hoover, the incumbent, was blamed for the Depression. His faith in voluntary cooperation and balanced budgets seemed heartless to a nation in free fall. Unemployment reached twenty-three percent by election day; breadlines and Hoovervilles—shanty towns—were ubiquitous symbols of the administration's perceived failure. Hoover campaigned defensively, warning that Roosevelt's programs would threaten the free market; the message fell flat.

Franklin D. Roosevelt promised action: the only thing we have to fear is fear itself, and a willingness to experiment with government intervention. FDR won forty-two of forty-eight states and carried the first explicitly Democratic congressional majorities in decades. The Democratic base shifted: southern conservatives remained, but urban workers, immigrants, intellectuals, and the unemployed became the party's core.

The election ushered in twenty years of Democratic dominance and the welfare state: Social Security, labor organizing, public works. The New Deal Coalition—urban Catholics, Jews, blacks, farmers, unionists—kept the Democrats in power through nineteen sixty-eight. Social Security would be created in nineteen thirty-five by the New Deal this election made possible.
